title: Morning After Moonlight
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 11 of 40
content:
Morning arrived with a stiff neck, cold coffee, and Greg's arm wrapped around my waist.

The van was warmer than the night had been, but not by much. My cheek rested against the worn fabric of his shirt. His heartbeat moved beneath it, steady and unhurried. For a few minutes, I stayed still and let myself believe that waking beside someone could be ordinary.

Then Greg's phone rang.

He groaned, reached blindly across me, and knocked a thermos onto the floor. It rolled beneath the front seats.

“If that is a telemarketer,” he muttered, “I am going to sell them a van.”

The phone rang again.

I lifted my head. “You should answer.”

“I should do many things.”

“Like retrieving the coffee.”

“The coffee has made its choice.”

He found the phone beneath the seat and squinted at the screen. His expression shifted from sleepy affection to startled panic.

“It’s Steven,” he said.

“Your son?”

“Yes.”

“Do you want me to—”

“No, stay.”

The request came too quickly to be casual. Greg answered.

“Hey, buddy.”

The voice on the other end was muffled, but bright. Greg's shoulders relaxed.

“No, I’m not in trouble.” He glanced at me. “I’m at the overlook.”

Steven said something that made Greg rub his face.

“I did not forget. I told you I would call after the gig.”

Another pause.

“I know. I’m sorry.”

The tenderness in his voice was different from the way he spoke to me, but not separate from it. I listened to the care he gave freely, the ease with which he admitted fault.

“I’ll call tonight,” Greg promised. “Love you too.”

He ended the call and exhaled.

“He’s okay?” I asked.

“Yeah. He’s visiting a friend and wanted to hear about the show.” Greg put the phone down. “He knows about you.”

I sat up. “What?”

“Not everything.” His ears went pink. “I told him I met someone.”

“When?”

“A few days ago.”

“You told your son about me before I knew you had told anyone?”

“I didn’t mean to make it weird.”

“I’m not sure you get to decide whether it’s weird.”

Greg's face fell. I immediately regretted the sharpness, but the feeling underneath it remained.

“I’m sorry,” I said. “I’m not angry that he knows. I’m surprised.”

“I was excited.”

The simple confession disarmed me.

“You were excited?”

“I wanted someone to know I was happy.”

The van became very quiet.

I looked at him. He had spent so much of his life turning pain into music, but happiness still seemed to make him nervous. As though naming it might invite the universe to take it back.

“I’m happy too,” I said.

His eyes searched mine. “You are?”

“Yes.”

“Even though I told your existence to my son before asking permission?”

“I’m going to continue being annoyed about that for at least another hour.”

“Fair.”

“But yes.”

Greg reached for my hand. “Would you want to meet him?”

The question carried more weight than the words showed. It was not a demand. It was a door he was opening.

“Do you want me to?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because he’s important to me. And you are.”

I looked out through the open van doors. Morning had begun to color the horizon.

“I’m nervous,” I admitted.

“Steven is very friendly.”

“That might be worse.”

“He also talks a lot when he’s nervous.”

“Is he like you?”

“He is like himself.” Greg smiled. “But he got the talking from me.”

“What if he doesn’t like me?”

“Then we give him time. He doesn’t have to like you immediately. Neither did you.”

“I liked you at breakfast.”

“You liked the pancakes.”

“The pancakes were influential.”

Greg's thumb moved over my knuckles.

“He’ll be okay,” Greg said. “And if it’s too much, we leave. You don’t have to perform being comfortable.”

I looked at him. “Do you tell everyone that?”

“Only people I want to keep.”

The words made the morning softer.

I spent the day in Beach City instead of returning to the studio. Greg brought me to the car wash, where he introduced me to the hose as though it were a respected colleague. I helped him replace the broken leg on the record shelf. The repair was uneven, but the shelf stood.

“A triumph,” Greg said.

“A warning.”

“Both can be true.”

That evening, Steven arrived at the boardwalk carrying a backpack and a smile bright enough to compete with the sunset. He was taller than I expected, with the same kind eyes as the boy in the photograph, though his face had grown into itself.

“Hi!” he said.

I said hello.

Steven hugged me before asking, then stopped halfway and lifted both hands. “Sorry. Is hugging okay?”

The question made me smile.

“Yes,” I said.

He hugged me carefully, briefly, and stepped back.

“Dad has been talking about you,” Steven said.

Greg groaned. “Have I?”

“You said they laugh at your worst jokes.”

“That was private.”

“You also said they make tea too hot.”

“That was observational.”

“And that they think the van is a house with delusions.”

Steven turned to me. “I like you.”

I laughed. Greg covered his face.

The three of us walked the boardwalk. Steven asked about my move, my favorite music, and whether I had seen the lighthouse. He listened to every answer. When I asked about him, he gave me stories that were stranger than anything I could have imagined and somehow told them with complete sincerity.

Greg watched the two of us talk. Pride softened his whole body.

At the pier, Steven bought three ice creams. One melted down his wrist before he could eat it.

“You have to lick it faster,” Greg advised.

“I know how ice cream works, Dad.”

“I’m offering support.”

“You’re making it worse.”

“That’s my specialty.”

I wiped a drop of melting ice cream from my hand. Steven offered me a napkin. Greg offered me his sleeve. I chose the napkin.

“Wise,” Steven said.

“I’m learning.”

As the sun went down, Steven received a message and prepared to leave. He hugged Greg first, then turned to me.

“I’m glad Dad found you,” he said.

My chest tightened. “You barely know me.”

“I know he smiles differently.”

I looked at Greg. He was pretending to study the horizon.

“He’s always smiled,” I said.

“Not like that.”

Steven hugged me again, then walked toward the road.

Greg waited until his son was out of earshot. “I’m sorry.”

“For what?”

“He’s very perceptive.”

“That’s not a crime.”

“It should be. He uses it against me.”

I slipped my hand into Greg's. “Your son is wonderful.”

Greg's fingers tightened around mine.

“Thank you for meeting him,” he said.

“Thank you for asking.”

“I should have asked before telling him.”

“Yes.”

“I’m still going to be happy about it.”

“You’re allowed.”

He looked at me, sunlight fading across his face. “Can I kiss you?”

“Your son is still on the boardwalk.”

“That was not an answer.”

I leaned closer. “Later.”

Greg smiled. “I can work with later.”

They walked home beneath the first stars. Greg's hand stayed in mine, and for once, the future did not feel like a door I had to open alone.

The next morning, Steven sent me a message from somewhere with too much sunlight.

HI! DAD SAYS YOU LIKE TEA. I FOUND A TEA SHOP THAT SELLS TEA THAT CHANGES COLOR. I THINK IT MIGHT BE MAGIC BUT IT COULD ALSO BE FOOD DYE. DO YOU WANT SOME?

I showed Greg.

“He gets that enthusiasm from me,” Greg said.

“He gets the all-caps from you too?”

“No. That’s new.”

I typed back: YES, PLEASE. TELL YOUR DAD TO STOP TELLING PEOPLE MY TEA HABITS.

Steven answered almost immediately: HE SAYS HE WILL NOT.

Greg took the phone from me and typed: TRAITOR.

The three of us exchanged messages for nearly an hour. Steven sent pictures of the tea. Greg sent a picture of the terrible pancake he had attempted to make in the motel kitchenette. I sent a photograph of the crooked bookshelf.

Steven replied: IT LOOKS LIKE IT HAS STORIES.

“He’s very kind,” I said.

“He gets that from his mother.”

The words were not bitter. They were tender, carrying the memory of someone absent without turning the absence into a wound I had to manage.

I put the phone down. “Thank you for letting me meet him.”

“Thank you for wanting to.”

Greg's hand found mine beneath the blanket.

“I was afraid,” I said.

“I know.”

“I’m still afraid.”

“I know.”

“But I’m glad I did it.”

He kissed my knuckles. “That’s usually how courage works.”

“You’re going to make it a lesson.”

“I’m going to make it breakfast.”

He attempted pancakes again. The first was burnt. The second was raw. The third was shaped like a star and tasted surprisingly good.

“You made a star,” I said.

“It happened naturally.”

“It’s an omen.”

“It’s breakfast.”

We ate it together, the two of us sitting on the motel bed while sunlight filled the room.

Later, when Greg drove I home, Steven called. I listened as they argued about whether a magical lion could be trained to stop sitting on the passenger seat. Greg put the call on speaker. When Steven asked me to take his side, I refused on the grounds that I had insufficient evidence.

“You’re learning family politics,” Greg said.

“I’m learning not to get between you and the lion.”

“Very wise.”

The van rolled into Beach City. Greg's hand rested on my knee.

I had not planned to meet his son when I arrived with my suitcase. I had not planned to fall in love with a man who carried a guitar like a second heartbeat.

The best parts of my life had begun without plans.
